passages.source_text: Ὀρθριαίτερον δὲ πολλῷ τοῦ καθ’ ἡμέραν ὁ Πέτρος διυπνισθεὶς εἰσῄει πρὸς ἡμᾶς καὶ ἐξυπνίσας ἔφη Φαυστῖνος καὶ Φαυστινιανὸς ἅμα Κλήμεντι μετὰ τῶν οἰκείων ἀκολουθησάτωσάν μοι, ὅπως ἐν σκεπινῷ τῆς θαλάσσης τόπῳ ἐλθόντες ἐν ἀκατασκόπῳ βαπτίσαι αὐτὴν δυνηθῶμεν. πλὴν ἐπὶ τὸν αἰγιαλὸν γενομένων ἡμῶν μεταξύ τε πετρῶν τινῶν γαληνοῦ καὶ καθαροῦ τόπου εὐπορεσάντων, ἐβάπτισεν αὐτήν. ἡμεῖς δὲ οἱ ἀδελφοί, τῶν γυναικῶν χάριν ἅμα ἀδελφῷ καὶ ἄλλοις τισὶν ὑποχωρήσαντες καὶ λουσάμενοι, ἐλθόντες ἔπειτα τὰς γυναῖκας παρελάβομεν. καὶ οὕτως ἐν κρυφαίῳ τόπῳ πορευθέντες εὐχόμεθα. ἔπειτα ὁ Πέτρος τὰς γυναῖκας διὰ τὸν ὄχλον προέπεμψεν, δι’ ἄλλης ὁδοῦ ἐπὶ τὴν ξενίαν ἐλθεῖν κελεύσας, ἀνδρῶν τε μόνοις ἡμῖν συνεῖναι τῇ μητρὶ καὶ ταῖς αὐταῖς γυναιξὶν ἐπέτρεψεν. ἐλθόντες οὖν εἰς τὴν ξενίαν καὶ ἀναμένοντες αὐτὸν ἐλθεῖν ἀλλήλοις διελεγόμεθα. μετὰ ἱκανὰς δὲ ὥρας ὁ Πέτρος ἐλθών, τὸν ἄρτον ἐπ’ εὐχαριστίᾳ κλάσας καὶ ἐπιθεὶς ἅλας, τῇ μητρὶ πρῶτον ἐπέδωκεν καὶ μετ’ αὐτὴν ἡμῖν τοῖς υἱοῖς αὐτῆς. καὶ οὕτως αὐτῇ συνειστιάθημεν καὶ τὸν θεὸν εὐλογήσαμεν.

τότε λοιπὸν ὁ Πέτρος τὸν ὄχλον εἰσεληλυθότα ἰδὼν καὶ καθεσθεὶς καὶ παρακαθεσθῆναι ἡμᾶς κελεύσας ὑφηγεῖται τὰ πρῶτα πείθων ἡμᾶς τίνι λόγῳ προπέμψας ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος καὶ αὐτὸς βραδύνας ἐπῆλθεν. τὴν δὲ αἰτίαν ἔλεγεν τοιαύτην. ἅμα τῷ ὑμᾶς (φησὶν) ἀποστῆναι, γέρων συνεισῄει ἐργάτης, περιέργως κλέπτων ἑαυτόν, προκατασκοπήσας ἡμᾶς (ὡς αὐτὸς ὕστερον ὡμολόγει) πρὸς τὸ ἰδεῖν τί ἂν πράττοιμεν εἰς τὸν σκεπινὸν τόπον εἰσελθόντες, λάθρα ἐκβὰς ἠκολούθησεν. καὶ ἐν εὐκαίρῳ τόπῳ προσελθὼν καὶ προσαγορεύσας ἔφη Ἐκ πολλοῦ σοι ἀκολουθῶν καὶ συντυχεῖν θέλων ᾐδούμην μήπως ὡς περιέργῳ μοι χαλεπαίνῃς, νῦν δὲ τὰ ἐμοὶ δοκοῦντα ἀληθῆ, εἰ βούλει, λέγω. κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην Λέγε ἡμῖν ὅπερ σοι δοκεῖ καλὸν εἶναι, καὶ ἀποδεξόμεθά σε, κἂν τῷ ὄντι μὴ καλὸν ᾖ τὸ λεγόμενον, ἐπείπερ ἀγαθῇ προαιρέσει τὸ δοκοῦν σοι καλὸν εἰπεῖν ἠθέλησας.

καὶ ὁ γέρων τοῦ λέγειν ἤρξατο οὕτως· Θαλάσσῃ ὑμᾶς λελουμένους εἰς τὸν ἀπόκρυφον τόπον ὑποχωρήσαντας ἰδών, προσελθὼν λάθρα κατεσκόπουν τὸ τί ἂν ἐν κρυφαίῳ εἰσιόντες πράττοιτε, καὶ ἐπειδὴ εὐχομένους εἶδον, ὑπεχώρησα· ἐλεήσας δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀνέμεινα, ὅπως ἐξιοῦσιν προσομιλήσας πείσω μὴ ἀπατᾶσθαι. οὔτε γὰρ θεός ἐστιν οὔτε πρόνοια, ἀλλὰ γενέσει τὰ πάντα ὑπόκειται, ὡς ἐγὼ ἐφ’ οἷς πέπονθα πεπληροφόρημαι, ἐκ πολλοῦ ἀκριβῶν τὸ μάθημα. μὴ οὖν ἀπατῶ, τέκνον. εἴτε γὰρ εὔχῃ εἴτε μή, τὰ ἐκ τῆς γενέσεως πάσχειν ἀνάγκην ἔχεις· εἰ γὰρ εὐχαί τι ἐδύναντο ἢ τὸ εὖ ποιεῖν, αὐτὸς ἂν ἐν τοῖς κρείττοσιν ἤμην. καὶ νῦν εἰ μή σε ἀπατᾷ ἡ πενιχρά μου αὕτη ἐσθής, οὐκ ἀπιστήσεις οἷς λέγω. ἐν πολλῇ βίου ποτὲ ὢν περιουσίᾳ, πολλὰ καὶ θεοῖς ἔθυον καὶ δεομένοις παρεῖχον, καὶ ὅμως εὐχόμενός τε καὶ εὐσεβῶν τὴν πεπρωμένην ἐκφυγεῖν οὐκ ἠδυνήθην. κἀγὼ ἔφην Τίνα ἐστὶν ἃ πέπονθας; ὁ δὲ ἀπεκρίνατο Οὐκ ἀνάγκη λέγειν νῦν, ἴσως ἐπὶ τέλει ἀκούσει τίς τε ὢν ἐγὼ καὶ τίνων ἐν ποίαις βίου περιστάσεσιν γέγονα. νῦν δὲ ὅτι γενέσει τὰ πάντα ὑπόκειται, πληροφορηθῆναί σε θέλω.

κἀγὼ ἔφην Εἰ γενέσει τὰ πάντα ὑπόκειται καὶ τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχειν πεπληροφόρησαι, σεαυτῷ ἐναντία νοῶν συμβουλεύεις. εἰ μὲν γὰρ παρὰ γένεσιν οὐ δυνατὸν οὐδὲ τὸ φρονεῖν, τί ματαιοπονεῖς συμβουλεύων γενέσθαι ὃ γενέσθαι ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν; ἀλλ᾽ ἔτι μὴν εἰ γένεσις ὑφέστηκεν, μὴ σπεῦδε πείθειν ἐμὲ μὴ σέβειν τὸν καὶ τῶν ἄστρων δεσπότην, οὗ θέλοντος καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι τι, γενέσθαι δυνατόν. αἰεὶ γὰρ τὸ ὑποκείμενον τῷ ἡγουμένῳ πείθεσθαι ἀνάγκην ἔχει. τὸ μέντοι τοὺς νομιζομένους θεοὺς σέβειν, γενέσεως ἐπικρατούσης, περιττόν ἐστιν. οὔτε γὰρ παρὰ τὸ δοκοῦν τῇ πεπρωμένῃ τι γίνεται οὔτε αὐτοί τι ποιεῖν δύνανται, τῇ καθόλου αὐτῶν ὑποκείμενοι γενέσει. εἰ γένεσις ἐστιν, ἀντίκειται τὸ μὴ πρῶτον ἄρχειν. ὑποκεῖσθαι οὐ δύναται ὡς ἀγένητον ἑαυτοῦ πρεσβύτερον μηδὲν ἔχον.

τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους λεγόντων ἡμῶν, πολὺς παρέστη ὄχλος. καὶ τότε ἐγὼ εἰς τὸν ὄχλον ἀποβλέπων ἔφην Ἐγὼ καὶ τὸ ἐμὸν φῦλον ἐκ προγόνων θεὸν σέβειν παρειληφὼς καὶ παράγγελμα ἔχων γενέσει μὴ προσανέχειν (λέγω δὴ τῷ τῆς ἀστρολογίας μαθήματι), διὰ τοῦτο οὐ προσέσχον. ὅθεν ἀστρολογίας μὲν οὐκ εἰμὶ ἔμπειρος, ὧν δὲ εἰμί, ὑφηγήσομαι. ἐπειδὴ γένεσιν ἀπὸ αὐτῆς τῆς κατὰ τὴν γένεσιν ἐπιστήμης ἀνασκευάζειν οὐ δύναμαι, βούλομαι ἄλλῳ τρόπῳ ἀποδεῖξαι ὅτι κατὰ πρόνοιαν διοικεῖται τὰ πράγματα καὶ ἕκαστος πρὸς ἃ πράττει τιμῆς ἢ κολάσεως τεύξεται, εἴτε νῦν εἴτε αὖθις, οὐδέν μοι διαφέρει, πλὴν ὅτι πάντως ἀπολαύσει ἕκαστος ὧν ἔπραξεν. ἡ δὲ ἀπόδειξις τοῦ μὴ εἶναι γένεσιν ἔστιν αὕτη. τῶν παρεστώτων εἴ τις ὀφθαλμῶν ἐστέρηται ἢ κυλλὴν τὴν χεῖρα ἔχει ἢ χωλὸν τὸν πόδα ἢ ἕτερόν τι περὶ σῶμα, ὃ ὑποστροφὴν πρὸς ἴασιν πάλιν οὐκ ἔχει καὶ παντὸς ἰατικοῦ ἐπαγγέλματος ἐκτός ἐστιν, ὃν οὐδὲ ἀστρολόγοι ἰᾶσθαι ἐπαγγέλλονται, ὅτι μὴ ἀπὸ τοῦ μακροῦ αἰῶνος τοιοῦτόν τι γέγονεν, ἐγὼ δὲ θεοῦ δεηθεὶς τὴν ἴασιν παράσχω, ὁπότε ἐκ γενέσεως κατόρθωσιν τὸ τοιοῦτο οὐδέποτε λαβεῖν ἠδυνήθη — τούτου οὕτως γενομένου οὐχ ἁμαρτάνουσιν οἱ τὸν πάντα δημιουργήσαντα θεὸν βλασφημοῦντες; καὶ ὁ γέρων ἀπεκρίνατο Βλασφημεῖν γὰρ ἐστὶν τὸ λέγειν γενέσει ὑποκεῖσθαι τὰ πάντα; κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην Καὶ πάνυ· εἰ γὰρ πᾶσαι αἱ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἁμαρτίαι καὶ ἀσέβειαι καὶ ἀσέλγειαι ἐξ ἀστέρων γίνονται, οἱ δὲ ἀστέρες ταῦτα ποιεῖν ὑπὸ θεοῦ ἐτάγησαν, ἵνα πάντων χαλεπῶν ἀποτελεστικοὶ γένωνται: αἱ πάντων ἁμαρτίαι εἰς αὐτὸν ἀναφέρονται, τὸν τὴν γένεσιν θέντα ἐν τοῖς ἄστροις.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: Peter woke much earlier than his daily custom, came in to us, woke us, and said, “Let Faustinus and Faustinianus, together with Clement and the members of the household, follow me, so that we may go to a sheltered place by the sea and baptize her where no one can watch.” We went to the shore, found a calm, clean place among some rocks, and he baptized her. We brothers withdrew for the women’s sake, together with a brother and some others, bathed, and then came back and took the women with us. Going in this way to a hidden place, we prayed. Then, because of the crowd, Peter sent the women ahead, directing them to go by another road to the lodging, and permitted only us among the men to accompany our mother and those same women. We went to the lodging and spoke with one another while waiting for him to come. After a considerable number of hours Peter arrived, broke the bread with thanksgiving, put salt on it, and gave it first to our mother and then to us, her sons. Thus we dined with her and blessed God.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The source has singular ἀδελφῷ after the plural brothers. An additional fellow member of the community may be intended; he is left unnamed rather than silently omitted or identified as Peter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν ἄρτον ἐπ’ εὐχαριστίᾳ κλάσας καὶ ἐπιθεὶς ἅλας
lexical_decisions.chosen: broke the bread with thanksgiving, put salt on it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The thanksgiving and salt are both explicit. The text is not supplemented with wine or made an explicit identification of a later eucharistic rite.

passages.text: Then, seeing that the crowd had come in, Peter sat down, told us to sit beside him, and began by explaining why he had sent us ahead from the baptism and had himself arrived late. He gave the following reason: “As soon as you withdrew,” he said, “an old laborer came in with us, inquisitively concealing himself. Having watched us beforehand, as he later admitted, to see what we would do when we entered the sheltered place, he came out secretly and followed. At a suitable place he approached, greeted me, and said, ‘I have followed you for a long time, wanting to speak with you, but I was ashamed, lest you be angry at me for being inquisitive. Now, if you wish, I will tell you what seems true to me.’ I answered, ‘Tell us what you think is good, and we will welcome you, even if what is said is not actually good, since with a good intention you have wanted to say what seems good to you.’”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive use of “steal” means hiding or stealing along rather than theft of property. The note preserves the figurative wording’s furtiveness.
The object is the man, not necessarily an endorsement of the truth of his statement, as the following concession makes clear.

passages.text: “The old man began speaking in this way: ‘When I saw that you had bathed in the sea and withdrawn to the hidden place, I secretly approached and watched to see what you would do on entering a concealed place. When I saw you praying, I withdrew. Pitying you, however, I waited so that I might speak to you as you came out and persuade you not to be deceived. For there is neither God nor providence; everything is subject to destiny assigned at birth. I am fully convinced of this from what I have suffered, having studied the discipline carefully for a long time. So do not be deceived, child. Whether you pray or not, you are bound to suffer what comes from natal destiny. For if prayers or doing good had any power, I myself would be in better circumstances. Now, if this poor clothing of mine does not mislead you, you will not disbelieve what I say. Once, when I had great material abundance, I sacrificed much to the gods and provided much for the needy; yet, though I prayed and acted reverently, I could not escape what was fated.’ I said, ‘What have you suffered?’ He answered, ‘There is no need to speak of it now. Perhaps at the end you will hear who I am, whose family I belong to, and in what circumstances of life I have come to be. For now I want you to be fully convinced that everything is subject to natal destiny.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: destiny assigned at birth / natal destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένεσις literally refers to birth or origin; in this discussion it denotes fate inferred from a nativity or astrological birth configuration. The later explicit reference to astrology supports this contextual rendering, not a blanket substitution for every use of the word.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε γὰρ θεός ἐστιν οὔτε πρόνοια
lexical_decisions.chosen: For there is neither God nor providence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The denial is the old man’s stated position, not an assertion added by the narrator or translator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίς τε ὢν ἐγὼ καὶ τίνων
lexical_decisions.chosen: who I am, whose family I belong to
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elliptical plural genitive can concern ancestry or kin. It is not supplied as a particular named family.

passages.text: “I said, ‘If everything is subject to natal destiny and you are fully convinced that this is so, your advice reflects thoughts contrary to your own. For if even thinking cannot occur contrary to natal destiny, why do you labor in vain, advising that something happen which cannot happen? Moreover, even if natal destiny has existence, do not hurry to persuade me not to worship the master of the stars as well, at whose will even what is not to happen can happen. For what is subordinate must always obey its ruler. Worshiping the supposed gods, however, is superfluous if natal destiny prevails. For nothing happens contrary to what seems good to fate, nor can they themselves do anything, being subject to their universal natal destiny. If natal destiny exists, it is incompatible with not ruling first. It cannot be subordinate, since, being ungenerated, it has nothing older than itself.’”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ θέλοντος καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι τι, γενέσθαι δυνατόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: at whose will even what is not to happen can happen
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the negated infinitive as characterizing an event not otherwise destined to happen; the final γενέσθαι then states that it can happen at the ruler’s will. This supplies the contextual relation to destiny in English, not a Greek emendation. Another possible linkage places μὴ γενέσθαι directly within what the ruler wills: “when he wills even that something not happen, its happening is possible.” That is more difficult in the argument, but the negation’s attachment is not uniquely established here. The main text does not omit either occurrence of “happen” or the negative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ γένεσις ἐστιν, ἀντίκειται τὸ μὴ πρῶτον ἄρχειν. ὑποκεῖσθαι οὐ δύναται ὡς ἀγένητον ἑαυτοῦ πρεσβύτερον μηδὲν ἔχον
lexical_decisions.chosen: If natal destiny exists, it is incompatible with not ruling first. It cannot be subordinate, since, being ungenerated, it has nothing older than itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional is retained. The nearest named referent is natal destiny, read as the ungenerated principle hypothesized by fatalism. The neuter ἀγένητον can refer to an understood principle rather than agree directly with feminine γένεσις. A reference back to God or an ungenerated divine principle is also possible and would change which ruler is said to be unsubordinated. The pronoun “it” deliberately does not add a noun identifying the unexpressed subject uniquely.

passages.text: “As we were saying such things to one another, a large crowd gathered. Then, looking at the crowd, I said, ‘I and my people have inherited from our ancestors the worship of God and have a command not to attend to natal destiny—I mean the discipline of astrology. For this reason I have paid it no attention. Thus I am not experienced in astrology; I will explain the things in which I am experienced. Since I cannot refute natal destiny from the very science concerning natal destiny, I wish to demonstrate in another way that affairs are governed by providence, and that everyone will receive honor or punishment according to what he does. Whether now or later makes no difference to me, provided that everyone will certainly receive the consequences of what he has done. Here is the proof that natal destiny does not exist. If someone standing here lacks eyes, has a crippled hand, a lame foot, or some other bodily condition that has no possibility of returning to health and lies beyond every profession of healing—someone whom even astrologers do not profess to heal, because nothing of this sort has happened throughout the long span of time—and I, by petitioning God, provide the healing, when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny: if this happens in this way, are not those who blaspheme the God who made everything doing wrong?’ The old man answered, ‘Is saying that everything is subject to natal destiny blasphemy?’ I answered, ‘Very much so. For if all people’s sins, acts of impiety, and licentious deeds come from stars, and the stars were appointed by God to do these things, so that they bring about every grievous thing, everyone’s sins are referred back to him who placed natal destiny in the stars.’”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The source denotes a people or tribe; its proper name is not supplied in the English.
This can refer to every promise or claim of healing as well as a healing occupation. The main text keeps the claim that the condition lies beyond professed healing ability.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁπότε ἐκ γενέσεως κατόρθωσιν τὸ τοιοῦτο οὐδέποτε λαβεῖν ἠδυνήθη
lexical_decisions.chosen: when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: The hypothetical demonstration’s premise is retained as Peter’s argument. No actual present healing or empirical validation is asserted by the translation.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
